idiom_name: concrete public method delegating to a `T: Hook` field (sealed hook trait for closed sets)
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, so NVI is rebuilt as composition: the public type owns a collaborator that implements a small hook trait, and its inherent method performs the invariant and forwards. Generic bounds give static dispatch (monomorphised, no vtable) while Box<dyn Hook> gives a runtime-swappable extension point. Sealing the hook trait (pub trait Hook: private::Sealed) closes the set of implementations so the wrapper can rely on the hook contract - the Rust API Guidelines' C-SEALED pattern. Extension happens by supplying a different hook implementation; the wrapper's method cannot be overridden because the type is not inheritable.
pitfalls: A trait method with a default body can be overridden by any implementor, so a default method is not a non-virtual wrapper unless the trait is sealed (or partially sealed); keep the invariant in the concrete wrapper type.
Box<dyn Hook> costs an allocation and dynamic dispatch, while generic bounds monomorphise but leak the hook type into the public signature and grow code size.
Sealing relies on a private supertrait; if it is accidentally re-exported, downstream crates can implement the hook and the closed-world assumption breaks.

variants.name: Sealed trait: the provided default method is the wrapper
variants.idiom_name: trait with a wrapping default method + required hook methods, sealed against downstream impls
variants.implementation_notes: When the extension point must be a trait, the split can live inside the trait itself: the public method is a provided (default) implementation that performs the invariant and calls required hook methods, and the trait is sealed so only in-crate types may implement it - the crate then controls every implementation. Rust's standard traits use this shape (Write::write_all is a provided method built on the required write). Downstream callers may call the wrapper but cannot add implementations that bypass it; the 'final trait methods' pre-RFC (discussed alongside partial sealing via unnameable argument types) would make the guarantee first-class.
pitfalls: A default method stays overridable by every implementor; only sealing (or the unnameable-argument technique) keeps the wrapper authoritative, and the compiler has no final keyword for trait methods.
Sealing trades extensibility for the guarantee - if third parties must implement the hook, ship a separate unsealed hook trait instead.
An in-crate implementor can still override the default method; sealing protects the boundary, not the crate's own impls.
